# How rz-frida works

## Architecture

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    subgraph Host
        RZ[rizin] --> PLG[rz-frida plugin]
        PLG --> CORE[frida-core]
    end
    subgraph Device
        SRV[frida-server] --> PROC[target process]
        PROC --> AG[injected agent JS]
    end
    CORE <--> SRV
    AG --> PROC
```

The plugin is a rizin core plugin: it registers commands, owns one session
per rizin instance, and forwards every request through frida-core to the
target. On Android, frida-core talks to frida-server on the device, which
injects the **agent**: a JavaScript bundle running inside the target process
with the V8 engine.

The agent is loaded *lazily* on local attach: the first command that needs
it (for example `Frej` or `Frij`) injects it and waits for its boot
event (`agent.ready`). USB/remote spawn injects during `Froj` so
RegisterNatives can arm before resume. Pure host-side commands like
`Frsj` and `Fruj` never touch the target.

## The JSON envelope

`…j` commands reply with one of two shapes (`Frs` and `Fru` also
print plain text):

```json
{"ok":true,"result":{...}}
```

```json
{"ok":false,"error":{"code":"...","message":"..."}}
```

The error codes are stable strings: `invalid_uri`, `invalid_target`,
`timeout`, `cancelled`, `frida_unavailable`, `not_implemented`,
`internal_error`. Handlers return success even when the envelope carries an
error, so `ok:false` always reaches your scripts and pipelines.

## The session lifecycle

```{mermaid}
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> NEW: rz_frida_session_new
    NEW --> RESOLVED: Froj parses the URI
    RESOLVED --> ATTACHED: frida-core connects
    ATTACHED --> DETACHING: Frcj
    DETACHING --> CLOSED
    RESOLVED --> ERROR: connect failure
    ATTACHED --> ERROR: unexpected detach
    CLOSED --> [*]
    ERROR --> [*]
```

The declared states are `new`, `resolved`, `connecting`, `attached`,
`detaching`, `closed` and `error`. In practice the backend never publishes
`connecting`: a session goes from `resolved` straight to `attached` (or to
`error`). `Frsj` reports the current state.

The plugin keeps a **single session** per rizin instance. Opening a second
one while a session is active fails with `"a session is already open"`.
Close the current one with `Frcj` first.

Closing semantics:

- an **attached** target keeps running after `Frcj`
- a **launched** target keeps running
- a **spawned** target that was never resumed is **killed**

## Requests, replies and timeouts

Host and agent exchange JSON messages:

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as host (rizin)
    participant A as agent (target)
    H->>A: {id: 1, type: "ping", params: {}}
    A-->>H: {id: 1, ok: true, result: {...}}
    H->>A: {id: 2, type: "eval", params: {...}}
    A-->>H: {id: 2, ok: false, error: "..."}
    A-->>H: {type: "Fr.bp", ...}  (async event)
```

Requests carry an integer id and the agent replies with the same id, which
keeps asynchronous events from being mistaken for replies. The backend has a
single in-flight reply slot, so requests are serialized under a recursive
lock.

Every agent request respects `Fr.timeout` (5000 ms by default). On timeout
the host replies with `{"ok":false,"error":{"code":"timeout",...}}`. Ctrl-C
cancels a running request that registered the break hook with
`{"code":"cancelled",...}`. `Frrj` and `Frcj` do not use that
timeout/break hook the way `Froj` does.

Asynchronous events (breakpoint hits, watchpoint hits, RegisterNatives
captures, logs) do not block the host: they queue in a host-side buffer of 256
messages and are drained with `Frmj`. Older messages are dropped, and the
reply counts them in `dropped`.
